Population.evidence_source: [/page/6/Text/4] Many of our informants condemned themselves, blaming themselves for engaging in the suicidal act: "I know that God is against some of these things … a person killing himself when life is from God. I think I should not have done this because God will not be happy with me … " (man 2). This informant acknowledged that life is not to be taken by oneself and therefore blamed himself for attempting suicide. Another participant used the sixth commandment in the Bible to indicate that it is morally wrong to take one's life: "Thou shall not kill! … my judgment won't be easy … this is because I took my life. So it's not good" (woman 4).

Type.evidence_source: [/page/6/Text/4] Condemnation based on religious beliefs also featured in the responses of our informants and is an expression of understanding their own behaviour from within the religious moral system.

[/page/6/Text/5] According to Worthington (2003), to overcome self-condemnation, individuals who perceive themselves as offenders may not only generate self-forgiveness but also need someone else, from the outside, to forgive them. It is only then that the process of moral transformation could begin.
